hydro, wind and solar as the electricity they make.</li><li><b>Substitution.</b> Every MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts as the fuel a thermal plant would burn to make it.</li><li><b>Direct equivalent.</b> Every MWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts at its electricity, 3.6 GJ.</li><li><b>China.</b> China publishes 17.9% for primary electricity and other energy, in coal equivalent, a kind of substitution; by physical energy content its nuclear, hydro, wind and solar come to about 9.6% (the page's estimate).</li><li><b>Japan.</b> Japan's METI counts each kWh from nuclear, hydro, solar, wind and geothermal as 8.49 MJ, the fuel of a thermal plant at 42.4%, a kind of substitution. By physical content: 16.9 EJ, not 17.5; renewables 7.8%, not 12.0%.</li></ul><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you guess a country from its mix, switch between countries and conventions, turn on four lenses and open the regional cards.</p>

```{=html}
<li><b>As published.</b> Seven national balances from their official publishers (EIA, Eurostat, China's NBS, India's MoSPI, Japan's METI, Brazil's EPE, Statistics Norway), one data year each, read between 2 and 7 November 2026; converted to EJ with the UN's conventional factors.</li>
<li><b>Estimates.</b> China's physical-content figures are this page's partial estimate, and Japan's are this page's conversion of METI's balance; every real country's useful energy is a what-if at Prairieland's sector efficiencies. Each is labelled where it appears.</li>
<li><b>Illustrative.</b> Prairieland is fictional; its numbers are illustrative, from the course's shared national data.</li>
</ul></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Why the substitution method enlarges electricity</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<!-- f10-subst:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<ul class="f10-notes"><li><b>The rule.</b> A thermal plant at efficiency η burns 3.6 ÷ η PJ of fuel for each TWh it makes. Substitution counts every TWh from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar that way.</li><li><b>The factor.</b> 2.5 times its electricity at 40%, about 3 times at 33%.</li><li><b>Nuclear under physical content.</b> Its reactors' heat: measured where it is reported (the EU), from the plants' average heat rate (the U.S.), or electricity ÷ 0.33 where the heat is not known (India, Brazil, this page's China and Japan figures).</li><li><b>Recompute the share.</b> Substitution changes nuclear's assigned energy (electricity ÷ 0.40) and enlarges hydro, wind and solar, so the total changes too: the United States' nuclear is 8.5% by physical content, 6.7% by substitution.</li><li><b>Direct equivalent</b> counts every TWh at 3.6 PJ, so nuclear's energy falls to about a third of its physical-content value.</li><li><b>China's coal equivalent</b> is a substitution at the year's coal burned per kWh in thermal plants.</li><li><b>Japan's balance</b> is a substitution at 8.49 MJ per kWh, a thermal plant at 42.4%.</li></ul>
<!-- f10-subst:end -->
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Where each country's numbers come from</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<!-- f10-notes:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<table class="cf-two f10-prov"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Country and data year</th><th scope="col">Published</th><th scope="col">Counting method</th><th scope="col">Coverage</th><th scope="col">Changes on this page</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">United States, 2025</th><td data-l="Published">96.5 quads of primary energy consumption (Table 1.3).</td><td data-l="Counting method">Nuclear at its plants' average heat rate; hydro, wind, solar and geothermal electricity at 3,412 Btu per kWh since September 2023, close to physical energy content.</td><td data-l="Coverage">Final energy is EIA's end-use energy (Tables 2.2 to 2.5); it keeps gas lease and plant fuel in industry and pipeline fuel in transport (Table 4.3). Farms sit inside industry.</td><td data-l="Changes on this page">Non-fuel use (6.5 quads) shown apart as non-energy use; geothermal (0.117 quads) drawn as its own source; solar includes small-scale solar (Table 10.6).</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">European Union (27 countries), 2024</th><td data-l="Published">55,790 PJ of gross available energy.</td><td data-l="Counting method">Physical energy content: nuclear as reactor heat; hydro, wind and solar photovoltaic as their gross electricity (nrg_bal_peh).</td><td data-l="Coverage">Includes 1,704 PJ of fuel for international shipping, shown apart. Bioenergy is renewables less the other renewable sources, so it holds the renewable part of waste; non-renewable waste sits in 'other'.</td><td data-l="Changes on this page">Coal includes peat and oil shale; solar includes solar heat (164 PJ); geothermal, ambient heat and tide drawn as one source.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">China, 2023</th><td data-l="Published">571,327 × 10,000 t of coal equivalent (5.71 billion t, about 167 EJ): coal 54.8%, oil 18.8%, gas 8.5%, primary electricity and other energy 17.9%.</td><td data-l="Counting method">Coal equivalent: nuclear, hydro, wind and solar electricity counted at the coal burned per kWh in the year's thermal plants, a kind of substitution.</td><td data-l="Coverage">Partial: the 'other energy' inside NBS's 17.9% is not split by NBS and is left out. Final energy is not drawn.</td><td data-l="Changes on this page">Physical content is the page's estimate: fossil fuels as published, plus the four sources' TWh (nuclear ÷ 0.33). Solar from the 2023 Communiqué; the rest from the 2025 Yearbook.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">India, fiscal year 2023-24 (provisional)</th><td data-l="Published">903,158 ktoe (37,813 PJ) of total primary energy supply.</td><td data-l="Counting method">Hydro, wind and solar at their electricity (1 GWh = 0.086 ktoe); nuclear at its electricity ÷ 0.33.</td><td data-l="Coverage">No row for firewood or other traditional biomass: every share here is of the sources the balance covers.</td><td data-l="Changes on this page">Coal includes lignite; oil is crude oil less net exports of products. Wind, solar and other renewable power includes bio-power and small hydro. 'Other' final use is farms and non-specified uses.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Japan, fiscal year 2024 (April 2024 to March 2025)</th><td data-l="Published">17,461,344 TJ (17.5 EJ) of domestic primary energy supply, fiscal year 2024, final figures.</td><td data-l="Counting method">Fuels at their gross calorific value. Nuclear, hydro, solar, wind and geothermal electricity at 8.49 MJ per kWh, the fuel of a thermal plant at 42.4%: a kind of substitution.</td><td data-l="Coverage">Waste burned for energy, and heat and power recovered in industry (573,930 TJ), count as a source: the page keeps them, as neither renewable nor fossil.</td><td data-l="Changes on this page">Physical content is the page's conversion: each kWh at 3.6 MJ, nuclear's and geothermal's as heat (÷ 0.33, ÷ 0.10). Coal includes coal products; farms and fishing sit in industry.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Brazil, 2025</th><td data-l="Published">328.5 Mtep of domestic energy supply (Oferta Interna de Energia).</td><td data-l="Counting method">Hydro, wind and solar at their electricity (1 kWh = 860 kcal); nuclear at its electricity ÷ 0.33.</td><td data-l="Coverage">Bioenergy: sugarcane products 52.0, firewood and charcoal 27.1, black liquor and other renewables 29.2 Mtep. ## Check yourself
```
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: three myths, then four questions.</p>
<!-- f10-check:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f10-myth"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="share" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A country's renewable share of primary energy is a single, fixed number.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Norway's is 48% by physical energy content and 68% by substitution, for the same plants in the same year.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="exporter" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A country that produces more energy than it uses imports none.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Norway produced 2,593 TWh in 2025 and still imported 124 TWh, while exporting 2,380 TWh.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="useful" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If every country used energy at Prairieland's sector efficiencies, most of its primary energy would end up as useful heat, motion and light.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, in this what-if: for the six real countries drawn here, 43% to 48% of primary energy would become useful energy. Their real efficiencies differ and are not in official statistics.</p></details></div></div><div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f10"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="which" data-answer="a"><p class="lx-qtext">Which of the eight gets 60% of its primary energy from coal and lignite and imports 40% of its supply?</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">India</li><li data-value="b">The European Union</li><li data-value="c">Brazil</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>India (fiscal year 2023-24): coal and lignite 60% of the sources its balance covers (traditional biomass is not in the balance); net import dependency 40.27%, as MoSPI publishes it.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="mult" data-answer="b"><p class="lx-qtext">By substitution at 40% efficiency, 1 TWh of wind electricity (3.6 PJ) counts as how many PJ of primary energy?</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">3.6 PJ</li><li data-value="b">9 PJ</li><li data-value="c">10.9 PJ</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>3.6 ÷ 0.40 = 9.0 PJ: the fuel a thermal plant at 40% would burn to make it, 2.5 times the electricity.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="dep" data-answer="a"><p class="lx-qtext">The EU's import dependency was 57.3% in 2024. What does Eurostat divide by what?</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Net imports ÷ gross available energy</li><li data-value="b">Imports ÷ production</li><li data-value="c">Production ÷ gross available energy</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Net imports (imports less exports) ÷ gross available energy, the EU's primary energy.</p></details></div><div class="lx-qq" data-id="china" data-answer="c"><p class="lx-qtext">China publishes 17.9% for primary electricity and other energy, in coal equivalent. By physical energy content, nuclear, hydro, wind and solar come to about…</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">the same</li><li data-value="b">a little more</li><li data-value="c">about half as much</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 9.6% (the page's estimate): coal equivalent counts each kWh as the coal a thermal plant would burn, so NBS's figure is 2.6 times the four sources' electricity (it also holds some other energy).</p></details></div></div>
<!-- f10-check:end -->
```
